title: Reading a broken metal part: fatigue, fracture, corrosion, creep
description: Metal parts break in a few recognisable ways, and each one leaves clues on the broken face. Read real failure photos and learn to tell fatigue, brittle cleavage, ductile overload, corrosion, and creep apart.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: A part has broken in service. Before anyone replaces it, why is the fracture surface photographed?

options.text: Because it records where the crack started, which way it ran, and by what mechanism
Because it is the only way to check the alloy against its chemical specification
Because the surface texture reveals the part's manufacturing date
Because hardness can only be measured on a freshly broken face

questions.explanation:
Fractography reads the broken face as evidence. The face can show where the crack began, how it grew, whether it ran all at once or over many cycles, and sometimes what surrounded it. Handling the part, rubbing the halves together, or wire-brushing the face can wipe that record out, so photograph it first.

An investigation needs to know what happened and whether it will happen again. Fitting a new part without reading the old fracture answers neither question.

questions.title: This aluminium specimen was pulled until it broke. What does the narrow waist just below each broken end tell you?

images.alt: Two halves of a fractured aluminium tensile specimen held between finger and thumb, each end narrowing to a thinned waist below the break.
images.caption: Tensile test of an AlMgSi aluminium alloy. Photo by Sigmund, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Al_tensile_test.jpg).

images.alt: Two panels. The ductile bar has a thinned waist at the break and interlocking cup-and-cone faces; the brittle bar breaks flat at full width with faces that fit back together.
images.caption: Check for necking first. You can see it without any instrument.

options.text: The metal stretched and thinned a long way before anything separated
The specimen was machined with a taper before the test began
The break happened instantly, with no plastic flow at all
The alloy was too hard to deform, so it sheared off

questions.explanation:
The narrow waist is called necking. Once a tensile specimen passes its ultimate strength, the stretching concentrates in one band, and that band thins until it tears. Visible necking is the clearest sign of a ductile failure.

A ductile part may sag, bulge, or narrow before it breaks, and it absorbs a lot of energy on the way. Designers value that warning because it gives people time to react.

questions.title: These cast-iron halves have flat, grainy faces and still measure the full original diameter. What kind of failure is this?

images.alt: Two upright halves of a broken cast-iron tensile specimen photographed side by side, each with a flat, sparkling, granular fracture face at full bar diameter.
images.caption: A cast-iron tensile specimen: flat faces, full section, no waist. Photo by Sigmund, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cast_iron_tensile_test.JPG).

options.text: Brittle fracture. It separated with almost no plastic deformation
Ductile overload, with the necking hidden inside the specimen
Fatigue, after millions of small load cycles
Creep rupture after a long time at high temperature

questions.explanation:
A brittle fracture runs straight across the full section with no necking. Very little metal moved, so the halves fit back together, and the break absorbed far less energy than a ductile one would.

Brittleness depends on conditions as well as material. The same steel can be ductile when it is warm, loaded slowly, and smoothly shaped, then brittle when it is cold, loaded fast, or notched. Several early all-welded ships broke this way at low temperatures, starting from sharp corners, even though their steel and loads were ordinary.

questions.title: Why does the outer rim of a ductile tensile fracture slope at roughly 45° to the pulling direction?

images.alt: A necked bar broken into two interlocking halves beside a circular fracture face showing a stippled fibrous centre ringed by a sloping shear lip.
images.caption: Microvoids join up and tear open the centre. The rim finishes along the plane of maximum shear.

options.text: Because that is the plane on which shear stress is highest
Because that is the angle at which the test machine grips the specimen
Because it is a machining artefact left over from turning the bar
Because the rim cools faster than the centre and contracts at an angle

questions.explanation:
Pull a bar along its axis and the shear stress is highest on planes tilted 45° to it. In a ductile fracture, voids join up through the centre first. The crack then reaches the surface along those maximum-shear planes and leaves an angled rim.

That gives the classic *cup and cone*, with a shallow cup on one half and a matching cone on the other. A fibrous centre with a sloping shear lip on a round bar is strong evidence of ductile overload.

questions.title: This fracture surface is covered in shallow cavities a few micrometres across. What formed them?

images.alt: Electron micrograph of a steel fracture surface covered in overlapping cup-shaped cavities a few micrometres wide, with a fifteen micrometre scale bar.
images.caption: Ductile dimpled fracture in steel. Photo by Hausild, CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tv%C3%A1rn%C3%BD_lom.jpg).

options.text: Voids opened at particles inside the metal, grew under load, and merged
Gas bubbles that were trapped when the metal was cast
Corrosion pits etched into the surface after the part broke
Whole grains that were pulled apart along their boundaries

questions.explanation:
This is *microvoid coalescence*. Plastic strain opens small voids at inclusions and second-phase particles. The voids grow until the metal between them gives way and they join into a crack. Each dimple is half of a void, so the two fracture faces do not fit together.

Round dimples mean tension. Elongated dimples pointing in opposite directions on the two halves mean shear. Cleaner metal has fewer inclusions for voids to start at, so controlling inclusions can make a metal tougher.

questions.title: This surface is a patchwork of flat, shiny facets, each with a fan of fine lines. Which mechanism made it?

images.alt: Micrograph of a low-carbon steel fracture surface made of flat angular facets at many orientations, each crossed by fine branching river lines.
images.caption: Brittle cleavage in low-carbon steel, imaged with a confocal laser scanning microscope. Photo by DanilovVA, CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_brittle_fracture_surface_of_low-carbon_steel.jpg).

options.text: Cleavage. The crack split crystal planes through the grains
Microvoid coalescence, seen at low magnification
Fatigue striations from repeated loading
Cavities forming on grain boundaries during creep

questions.explanation:
Cleavage splits the metal along specific crystal planes instead of tearing it plastically. Each grain breaks into one flat facet. Neighbouring grains point different ways, so the facets catch the light at different angles and the surface looks crystalline.

The fine lines are *river patterns*. They form where the crack steps between planes at different levels, and they merge in the direction the crack was growing. Body-centred cubic metals such as ferritic steel cleave easily when cold, notched, or loaded fast. Face-centred cubic metals such as austenitic stainless steel and aluminium generally do not.

questions.title: What distinguishes a transgranular fracture from an intergranular one?

options.text: A transgranular crack cuts through the grains; an intergranular crack follows the boundaries between them
A transgranular crack happens in tension and an intergranular crack happens in compression
A transgranular crack starts at the surface and an intergranular crack starts inside
A transgranular crack is always slow and an intergranular crack is always fast

questions.explanation:
The terms describe the path the crack took, not its speed or the load direction. Cleavage and most fatigue cracks are transgranular and cut through the grains. Intergranular cracks run along grain boundaries and expose whole grain faces, which can look like sugar crystals.

If the crack followed the boundaries, something weakened them. Common causes are hydrogen, temper embrittlement, sensitisation, creep cavities, liquid-metal attack, and corrosion along the boundaries. That points the investigation toward chemistry or heat treatment.

questions.title: What are the fine, parallel ridges covering this fatigue fracture surface called?
questions.description: Answer with the term used in fractography. The scale bar in the image is 15 µm.

images.alt: Electron micrograph of a steel fatigue fracture surface showing dense fields of fine parallel ridges, with a fifteen micrometre scale bar.
images.caption: A field of fatigue striations on steel. Photo by Hausild, CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Striace.jpg).

questions.explanation:
These ridges are *striations*. One forms each time the crack tip blunts and sharpens again during a load cycle. They run perpendicular to the local growth direction, so they record both which way the crack went and how fast.

Striations are micrometres apart, so you need an electron microscope to see them. Broad bands you can see with the naked eye are beach marks, which are a different feature.

questions.title: In the regime where striations form, how many load cycles does a single striation represent?
questions.explanation:
Usually one striation marks one cycle. Their spacing gives the local crack-growth rate in millimetres per cycle, which helps estimate how long the crack grew and what load range drove it.

At very low stress intensity, several cycles can pass before the crack moves far enough to leave a visible ridge, so a striation count gives a minimum number of cycles. Not every alloy forms clear striations. Aluminium alloys and many steels do.

questions.title: Which statements about beach marks and striations are correct?

images.alt: A fracture face with a few broad curved bands beside a magnified panel showing dozens of fine parallel ridges, linked by lines from a small box on the fracture face.
images.caption: The same crack at two scales. One band visible to the eye can span a huge number of cycles.

options.text: Beach marks are usually visible without a microscope; striations are not
A single beach mark can span thousands or millions of cycles
Beach marks record a change in the loading, such as a shutdown, a rest, or an overload
Beach marks and striations are two names for the same feature at different magnifications
Counting beach marks gives you the number of load cycles the part survived

questions.explanation:
Both features are curved bands around the crack origin, at very different scales.

Striations are micrometre-scale and usually mark one cycle each. Beach marks, also called arrest or clamshell marks, are millimetre-scale bands left by a change in loading, such as a shutdown, a new duty cycle, an overload, or oxidation during a pause. A lab test at constant amplitude may leave no beach marks at all, and a few hundred beach marks can cover hundreds of millions of cycles.

questions.title: This aluminium bicycle crank broke during ordinary riding. Most of the face is bright and rough, and a darker region along one edge has curved lines on it. What happened?

images.alt: End-on view of a broken aluminium bicycle crank arm. Most of the fracture face is bright and coarsely crystalline; a darker, smoother crescent along the lower edge carries fine curved arrest lines.
images.caption: Fatigue fracture of a bicycle pedal crank. The dark crescent with arrest lines is the fatigue zone, and the bright area is the final overload. Photo by Lokilech, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pedalarm_Bruch.jpg).

images.alt: A circular fracture face labelled with three numbered zones: an initiation site at the rim, concentric beach marks across most of the section, and a hatched final fast fracture cap.
images.caption: Fatigue fractures in any part share these three zones.

options.text: A crack grew slowly through the dark region over many pedal strokes, then the rest gave way in one go
The whole section broke at once under a single enormous load
The dark region is where the metal overheated and melted
The crank was bent back and forth by hand until it tore, all in one ride

questions.explanation:
The dark fatigue zone started at the surface and grew a little with each pedal stroke. Rubbing and oxidation darkened and smoothed it, and the curved arrest marks bow away from the origin.

The bright, rough area is the final fast fracture. Once the crack had left too little metal, an ordinary pedal stroke broke the rest. The final load was nothing unusual.

questions.title: Two identical shafts both failed by fatigue. One face is almost all fatigue zone with a thin sliver of final fast fracture. The other is mostly final fast fracture. What does the difference tell you?

images.alt: Two circular fracture faces side by side. The left has a large shaded fatigue region and a thin final-fracture cap; the right has a small fatigue region and a large final-fracture area.
images.caption: Same part and same failure mode, but the final zones point to very different loads.

options.text: The one with the sliver was running at a lower stress
The one with the sliver was made from a weaker alloy
The one with the sliver was running at a higher temperature
Nothing useful; the ratio is random

questions.explanation:
A fatigue crack grows until the remaining metal can no longer carry the peak load of a cycle. At low stress, the crack has to grow through most of the section first, leaving a large fatigue zone and a thin final crescent. At high stress, a smaller crack is enough, so the final overload zone is larger.

Investigators use this ratio as an early clue. A large final zone suggests the part was working near its limit even when intact, so check the design and the duty as well as the crack.

questions.title: A bracket carries a repeated load whose peak is comfortably below the alloy's yield strength. Can it still fail by fatigue?

options.text: Yes. Fatigue cracks grow at nominal stresses far below yield
No, because nothing permanent happens below the yield strength
Only if the bracket is a polymer rather than a metal
Only if it is also above half the melting temperature

questions.explanation:
Nominal stress is the average over the whole section. At a notch, corner, scratch, or inclusion, the local stress can be several times higher, so a few grains can yield while the rest of the part does not. Each cycle leaves a little irreversible slip in those grains until a crack forms.

That is why a static strength check is not enough for a moving part. Fatigue commonly starts at nominal stresses well below yield, and it causes most mechanical failures in service.

questions.title: Where should you look first for the origin of a fatigue crack?

images.alt: Two stepped bars carrying force-flow lines. In the sharp-shouldered bar the lines pile into the square corner, marked with red bursts; in the filleted bar the same lines bend smoothly around a generous radius.
images.caption: Same material, load, and nominal stress. Only the corner changes the local stress.

options.text: A sharp internal corner or shoulder with no fillet radius
A keyway, cross-hole, or thread root
A stamped mark, tool witness line, or coarse machined finish
A corrosion pit
The middle of a large, smooth, polished face far from any change of section
A generously radiused transition that was shot peened after machining

questions.explanation:
Fatigue starts where stress concentrates. Changes of section, holes, thread roots, keyways, weld toes, stamped marks, and deep machining grooves all raise the local stress. A square shoulder can multiply it by three or more, and sharper features are worse.

Most fatigue cracks start at a free surface, so grinding marks, corrosion, and handling damage matter too. Generous radii and polished transitions lower the peak stress. Shot peening leaves the surface in residual compression, which makes it harder for each cycle to open a crack.

questions.title: A steel bracket and an aluminium bracket both survive ten million cycles on the test rig. Why is that result worth less for the aluminium one?

images.alt: An S-N plot with cycles to failure on a logarithmic axis. The steel curve reaches a horizontal fatigue limit; the aluminium curve keeps falling.
images.caption: The flat shelf is the difference. Steel has a stress it can survive indefinitely, and aluminium does not.

options.text: Aluminium alloys have no fatigue limit, so the S-N curve keeps falling and longer tests still find failures
Aluminium is not affected by cyclic loading in the first place
Fatigue data for aluminium is only meaningful below ten thousand cycles
Aluminium gets stronger the longer it is cycled

questions.explanation:
Plain carbon and low-alloy steels usually show a knee in the S-N curve somewhere between one and ten million cycles. Below this *fatigue limit*, life is effectively unlimited.

Aluminium alloys, copper alloys, and austenitic stainless steels have no knee. Their curves keep falling, so every stress amplitude has a finite life, and a fatigue strength only means something at a stated number of cycles. That is why aluminium airframes have finite design lives, retirement times, and inspection intervals instead of relying on an endurance limit.

questions.title: On the left is a coated, buried gas pipeline. On the right is the same spot after the corrosion product was blasted off. Why do engineers worry more about pitting than about uniform rusting?

images.alt: Two-panel photograph of a buried steel gas pipeline: on the left a dark patch of corrosion product on green coating beside a ruler, on the right the same area after abrasive blasting, showing shallow pits in bare steel.
images.caption: Before and after blasting. The pits were invisible until the corrosion product came off. Photo by Derek Mawhinney, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Corrosion.Pit.jpg).

options.text: A pit removes very little metal overall, yet it can perforate the wall at a single point
Pits spread across the surface faster than uniform corrosion does
Pits change the chemical composition of the alloy around them
Uniform corrosion cannot be measured, whereas pits can

questions.explanation:
Uniform corrosion thins the surface at a fairly predictable rate. Engineers can track it by weight loss or wall thickness and allow for it in the design. Pitting concentrates the metal loss in a few spots, so a pipe can lose very little mass overall and still leak.

Pits can hide under coatings, scale, or corrosion product until someone cleans the surface. Each pit is also a sharp notch where fatigue or stress corrosion cracking can start.

questions.title: Galvanised steel pipework is joined directly to brass and copper fittings, with water inside. Which metal corrodes?

images.alt: A wall-mounted water meter manifold in galvanised steel pipe joined to brass valves and copper pipework, with rust staining concentrated at the joints between the two metals.
images.caption: Galvanised steel joined directly to copper and brass, with the attack showing at the joints. Photo by Manuel Capdevila, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Steel-copper_galvanic_corrosion.jpg).

options.text: The zinc and steel. The less noble metal becomes the anode and dissolves
The copper and brass, because they are the softer metals
Both, at the same rate, since they sit in the same water
Neither, as long as the water is clean and fresh

questions.explanation:
Two different metals that touch and share the same electrolyte form a battery. The less noble metal becomes the anode, gives up electrons, and dissolves. The nobler metal is the cathode and stays protected.

Galvanising uses this on purpose. Zinc corrodes before steel and protects it even where the coating is scratched. Sacrificial anodes on ship hulls and in water heaters work the same way. Where you don't want the effect, a dielectric union between the two metals breaks the electrical path.

questions.title: Two joints sit in seawater: steel bolts holding a large copper plate, and copper bolts holding a large steel plate. Which one is the dangerous design?

images.alt: Two panels comparing a large anodic plate with three small cathodic fasteners against a large cathodic plate with three small anodic fasteners marked with red crosses.
images.caption: Both panels use the same metals. Only the area ratio is reversed, and that decides the outcome.

options.text: The steel bolts in the copper plate
The copper bolts in the steel plate
Both equally, because the metals are the same in each case
Neither, because a bolt is always the cathode

questions.explanation:
The areas control the corrosion rate. A large cathode can drive a lot of current, and a small anode concentrates that current into very little metal.

Steel bolts in a copper plate make a small anode next to a large cathode, so the bolts corrode fast. With copper bolts in a steel plate, the attack spreads thinly across the big steel plate. Avoid pairing a small piece of the less noble metal with a large piece of the nobler one. Steel fasteners in copper roofing or in graphite composites are common examples of this mistake.

questions.title: Fine branching cracks run out from a welded collar in this vessel wall. What has to be present at the same time for stress corrosion cracking?

images.alt: A cut section of vessel wall beside a welded collar, its surface covered by a dense network of fine branching cracks spreading out from the weld.
images.caption: Stress corrosion cracking driven by residual stress from an unsuitable welded reinforcement collar. Photo by CEphoto, Uwe Aranas, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Stress-Corrosion-Cracking-caused-by-weld-stress-01.jpg).

images.alt: Three overlapping circles labelled sustained tensile stress, susceptible alloy, and specific chemical environment, with stress corrosion cracking sitting only in the central overlap.
images.caption: Cracking happens only where all three circles overlap. Removing any one of them stops it.

options.text: A sustained tensile stress, which can come entirely from residual welding stress
An alloy that is susceptible to the particular environment involved
A specific chemical environment, such as chlorides for austenitic stainless steel
A load that cycles rapidly back and forth
A temperature above the alloy's melting point

questions.explanation:
Stress corrosion cracking (SCC) needs sustained tensile stress, a susceptible alloy, and a specific chemical environment, all at once. Take away any one and the cracking stops.

Residual stress from welding or cold forming can supply the tension with no applied load at all, which is why SCC often shows up near welds. The alloy and the environment have to match. Austenitic stainless steel cracks in hot chlorides but resists ammonia, and brass is the other way round. Fine, branching cracks with little deformation around them are a common visual clue.

questions.title: A steel part with a long, clean service record starts failing early after the equipment moves to a damp, salty site. The duty cycle is the same. What is the likeliest explanation?

images.alt: Three panels: a sound surface under cyclic load, the same surface with a corrosion pit forming a notch, and a fatigue crack growing down from the root of that pit.
images.caption: Corrosion makes the notch, and the ordinary cyclic load grows the crack.

options.text: Corrosion pits are forming and acting as ready-made crack starters
Salt water lowers the alloy's melting point
The humidity has increased the load the component carries
Steel loses its yield strength when it gets wet

questions.explanation:
A corrosion pit is a sharp notch, and fatigue cracks start easily at notches. In a corrosive environment, pits shorten or skip the long stage in which a crack would normally have to form.

Corrosion fatigue can also remove steel's fatigue limit. The S-N curve keeps falling instead of levelling off, so a stress that was safe in dry air now has a finite life. The fix may be a stated service life, a protective coating, or cathodic protection.

questions.title: A turbine blade under a constant load well below its yield strength slowly stretches over thousands of hours in service. What is that called?

images.alt: A strain-versus-time curve in three shaded bands: a decelerating primary stage, a long straight secondary stage, and an accelerating tertiary stage ending at a rupture cross.
images.caption: Most of the life is spent in the straight middle section. Once the curve turns upward, little life remains.

options.text: Creep
Fatigue
Cleavage
Work hardening

questions.explanation:
Creep is slow plastic deformation under a steady load. It has three stages. In the primary stage the rate slows as the metal work-hardens. The secondary stage runs at a steady minimum rate and takes up most of the life. In the tertiary stage, damage builds up faster and faster until rupture.

The design limit can be strain rather than fracture. A turbine blade that creeps a fraction of a millimetre can rub on its casing. A bolted flange that creeps can lose clamping force and leak before anything breaks.

questions.title: Creep becomes a design concern above roughly what fraction of a metal's absolute melting temperature?
questions.description: Answer as a decimal fraction, for example `0.25`. Both temperatures are measured in kelvin.
questions.explanation:
*Homologous temperature* is the service temperature divided by the melting temperature, both in kelvin. Above about 0.4, atoms diffuse fast enough for creep to matter.

Steel melts near 1700 K, which puts that threshold around 400 °C. Boiler tubes, steam pipes, and turbine blades can be limited by creep, but a steel bracket at room temperature is not. Lead melts near 600 K, so a lead roof sits near 0.5 on an ordinary day and can creep over decades. Solder joints and polymers have the same problem.

questions.title: Why does the strain rate speed up in the tertiary stage of creep?

options.text: Grain-boundary cavities and local thinning reduce the section carrying the load
The applied load is deliberately increased at that point in the test
The metal has begun to melt
The temperature is raised at the end to finish the test sooner

questions.explanation:
The load stays the same, but the material changes. Cavities form and join along grain boundaries while the section thins. Less metal carries the same force, so the true stress rises and the damage speeds up until the part ruptures.

Inspect high-temperature equipment for cavities and swelling during the secondary stage. Once tertiary creep starts, little service life remains.

questions.title: Which of these failure modes typically give little or no outward warning before the part separates?

options.text: Brittle cleavage fracture
Fatigue, right up until the final fast fracture
Stress corrosion cracking
Ductile overload

questions.explanation:
Ductile overload usually gives a warning. The part bends, sags, bulges, or necks and absorbs a lot of energy first. Designers may choose this behaviour even when it costs some strength.

Brittle fracture can run through a sound-looking part at close to the speed of sound. Fatigue cracks stay hidden for most of their growth. Stress corrosion cracks are fine, branching, and often covered by scale or coating. Parts at risk from these modes need damage-tolerant design and scheduled crack inspection with methods such as dye penetrant, magnetic particle inspection, or ultrasonics.

questions.title: A shaft snaps after three years in service. Two thirds of the face is smooth with fine curved lines, and the rest is rough. There is no necking anywhere. What is the diagnosis, and where should the fix go?

options.text: Fatigue under an ordinary repeated load. Remove the stress raiser at the crack origin
Ductile overload. Specify a stronger alloy
Brittle fracture from a single impact. Fit a guard
Creep. Reduce the operating temperature

questions.explanation:
Three years of service makes a one-off overload unlikely. The smooth zone with curved arrest lines is fatigue, and the rough zone is the final fast fracture. No necking rules out a slow ductile tear. The large fatigue zone also suggests the nominal stress was fairly low.

The fix belongs at the crack origin. With a notch present, a stronger steel does not bring a matching gain in fatigue strength, and stronger steels can be more notch-sensitive. Better fixes are a larger fillet, a smoother finish, shot peening, a redesigned keyway, or a lower stress range.
